newsitem.title: USA: Sun-Diamond barred from selling to government.
newsitem.headline: Sun-Diamond barred from selling to government.

text.p: The big California fruit concern Sun-Diamond was barred Friday from participating in all federal food purchase programmes for the next three years because of its recent criminal convictions for giving illegal gifts to a former Clinton cabinet member.

The Agriculture Department announced the ruling, which applies to all government agencies Sun-Diamond deals with. The decision could mean lost contracts worth millions of dollars to the nation's largest fruit cooperative.

"USDA is taking this action because of Sun-Diamond's recent federal court conviction for acts that seriously question the cooperative's business integrity or honesty," Robert Keeney of the department's Agricultural Marketing Service said in a statement.
"This action is being taken to protect the interests of the federal government," Keeney said.

Sun-Diamond, headquartered in Pleasonton, Calif., now has 30 days to appeal the decision before the Agriculture Department. A Sun-Diamond official said the company was confident the debarment action would be reversed.
"We believe that a thorough review of the record, and a fair application of the law will reverse this action," said Sandra McBride, communications manager for the company.

Sun Diamond was convicted last month in a federal court on eight criminal counts that included illegal gratuities to former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy in 1993 and 1994 and illegal campaign contributions to Espy's brother Henry.

The charges arose out of the government's two-year special investigation of the former Agriculture Secretary, who resigned in 1994 amid accusations he took illegal gifts and favours from companies the department regulated.
The ruling's impact, however, is not as bad as could be for the company, since Sun-Diamond's five affiliates were not included in the decision and can continue selling to the government.
"At this time, the government can still purchase products from Sun-Diamond affiliates," a government official said.
Sun-Diamond is owned by five member cooperatives, which are owned by about 4,500 farmers.
Sun-Diamond's affiliates, who have not been named in any criminal indictments, rank as the nation's largest raisin, prune, walnut, figs and apricot cooperatives.
The affiliates are Sun-Maid Growers of California, Diamond Walnut Growers Inc., Sunsweet Growers Inc., Valley Fig Growers and Hazelnut Growers of Oregon.
Not taking action against the affiliates is significant, since it is the individual cooperatives that actually sell their products to the Agriculture Department, not Sun-Diamond.
Sun-Diamond sells products to the Defence Department for government commissaries and military cafeterias. This will no longer be allowed under the ruling.
Data on how much Agriculture Department purchases from Sun-Diamond's affiliates, or how much the Defence Department buys from Sun-Diamond were unavailable.
